points.text: A straightforward implementation of multi-head attention creates separate query, key, and value weight matrices for each attention head, multiplies the input by each of them, and then proceeds with attention on each head separately.
This per-head approach is inefficient because the number of initial matrix multiplications grows with the number of heads.

A more efficient approach is to do one multiplication for queries, one for keys, and one for values using larger weight matrices, then split the resulting query, key, and value tensors into multiple heads.

After splitting the queries, keys, and values into heads, the remaining attention procedure stays the same: multiply queries by transposed keys to get attention scores, obtain attention weights, and multiply them by the values to get context vectors.
This more efficient implementation is called multi-head attention with weight splits.
Multi-head attention with weight splits is more computationally efficient than the earlier implementation.
In the earlier implementation, each attention head computed its own context vector and the context vectors from different heads were concatenated together.
In the previous code, there were separate classes for a multi-head attention wrapper and for causal attention, and the new implementation combines them into a single multi-head attention class.

In the weight-splitting approach, instead of multiplying the input by separate query matrices such as Wq1 and Wq2, the input is multiplied by one larger query matrix and the resulting queries are then split into components for different heads.
The larger query, key, and value weight matrices are sized so that their output dimension already includes the number of heads.
The output dimension satisfies D_out = head dimension × number of heads.
In the illustrated example, each head has dimension 2 and there are 2 heads, so the larger trainable query matrix has D_out = 4, which already includes the number of heads.
In the combined multi-head attention class, multiple heads are implemented by reshaping the query, key, and value tensors to split them into heads.
The forward method of the multi-head attention class takes an input tensor X and ultimately computes a context vector for each input embedding vector.
The input tensor to multi-head attention has three dimensions: batch size, number of tokens, and input dimension.
The input dimension D_in is the dimension of the embedding vector that represents each token.
For simplicity, the lecturer suggests thinking of tokens as words, such as “the,” “cat,” and “sleeps.”
In the example input of shape 1 × 3 × 6, there are 3 tokens, each represented by a 6-dimensional vector, and the batch size is 1.
The context output has one context vector per token, so its shape is number of tokens multiplied by D_out.
In the example, D_out is chosen to be 6, the same as D_in, which the lecturer says is typical in GPT-based models.
In the example, the number of attention heads is 2.
The head dimension is D_out divided by the number of heads.
In the example, head dimension = 6 / 2 = 3.
Since each head has dimension 3 and there are 2 heads, the total D_out is 6.
A required step is to initialize trainable weight matrices for the keys, queries, and values: W_k, W_q, and W_v.
The key, query, and value weight matrices must have first dimension D_in so that they are compatible with the input during matrix multiplication.
Therefore, the trainable key, query, and value matrices have shape D_in × D_out.
In the example, because D_in = 6 and D_out = 6, W_q, W_k, and W_v are 6 × 6 matrices.
In the code, the trainable weight matrices for query, key, and value are initialized in the constructor using neural network linear layers with dimensions D_in by D_out and bias set to zero.
The lecturer says a neural network linear layer is used for these weight matrices because it is optimized for initializing weights and is better for backpropagation later.
After initializing the trainable weight matrices, the input is multiplied by the query, key, and value weight matrices to produce the queries, keys, and values.
The input has shape 1 by 3 by 6, and multiplying it by each 6 by 6 query, key, or value weight matrix produces queries, keys, and values of shape 1 by 3 by 6.
In the 1 by 3 by 6 shape, 1 is the batch size, 3 is the number of tokens, and 6 is the output dimension D_out.
In the keys, queries, and values of shape 1 by 3 by 6, each row corresponds to one token and each token is represented by a six-dimensional vector.

In the code, the input is passed through the linear layers for key, query, and value, which applies the trainable weight matrices and produces keys, queries, and values with shape batch size by number of tokens by D_out.
A fourth tensor dimension is introduced because the three existing dimensions only represent batch size, number of tokens, and D_out, and do not represent the number of heads or the head dimension.
The head dimension equals D_out divided by the number of heads, so D_out equals head dimension multiplied by the number of heads.
The last dimension of the keys, queries, and values is reshaped to split D_out into number of heads and head dimension.
With D_out equal to 6 and the number of attention heads equal to 2, the head dimension is 3, so each 1 by 3 by 6 key, query, and value tensor is reshaped to 1 by 3 by 2 by 3.

A tensor of shape 1 by 3 by 2 by 3 can be interpreted by ignoring the batch dimension, then reading 3 as the number of tokens, 2 as the number of heads within each token, and 3 as the dimensionality of each head vector.
After reshaping, the keys and values also have shape 1 by 3 by 2 by 3.
The lecturer says you can think of two attention heads as two people paying attention to each token.

In the code, the last dimension is unrolled by calling view on the keys, queries, and values so that D_out is replaced by number of heads and head dimension, converting three-dimensional tensors into four-dimensional tensors.
Before transposition, tensors with shape 1 by 3 by 2 by 3 are grouped by tokens rather than by heads.
To compute attention scores, the tensors need to be grouped by the number of heads instead of by the number of tokens.

To group by heads, the number-of-tokens and number-of-heads dimensions are swapped so that the shape changes from batch, tokens, heads, head dimension to batch, heads, tokens, head dimension, which here is 1 by 2 by 3 by 3.
In the code, keys, queries, and values are transposed with transpose(1, 2) because Python uses zero-based indexing and dimensions 1 and 2 correspond to the number of tokens and the number of heads.
After transposition to shape 1 by 2 by 3 by 3, the tensors are grouped by head, so each head contains the token rows, and each token row contains a three-dimensional head vector.
Grouping by heads makes it possible to compute the attention score for each head separately, because there is a separate attention score matrix for each head before the results are concatenated.
The main reason for the transpose step is that grouping by tokens is not suitable for computing attention scores for each head in parallel, so the tensors are regrouped by heads.
Once the queries, keys, and values have the desired shape, the attention scores are computed using queries multiplied by keys transpose.
With the tensors grouped by head, multiplying queries by keys transpose automatically pairs head 1 of the queries with head 1 of the keys and head 2 of the queries with head 2 of the keys.
To compute query–key products, the key tensor must be transposed along its last two dimensions so that a row in the key matrix becomes a column.
After transposing the last two dimensions of the keys, the queries and transposed keys have compatible shapes for multiplication, and each head is multiplied only with the corresponding head.
Multiplying queries by transposed keys produces the attention score matrix.
The attention score tensor has dimensions batch size, number of heads, number of tokens, and number of tokens.

The last two dimensions of the attention scores are number of tokens by number of tokens because multiplying a number-of-tokens-by-head-dimension matrix by a head-dimension-by-number-of-tokens matrix yields a number-of-tokens-by-number-of-tokens matrix, while the first two dimensions stay the same.
Within each head, a row of the attention score matrix gives the attention scores between one query token and all tokens in the sequence.
For the example sentence "the cat sleeps," the second row corresponds to the query token "cat," and its entries represent attention between cat and "the," cat and "cat," and cat and "sleeps."
An attention score exists between each token and every other token, which is why each head’s attention matrix has number-of-token rows and number-of-token columns.
Attention scores are computed by multiplying the queries by the keys transposed along dimensions 2 and 3.
In the code, the attention score is implemented as the scaled dot product between queries and keys.
Each head has its own number-of-tokens-by-number-of-tokens attention score matrix.

To get attention weights from attention scores in causal attention, elements above the diagonal are replaced with negative infinity, the result is divided by the square root of the head dimension, and then softmax is applied row-wise.
In causal attention, a token should only attend to itself and earlier tokens, not to later tokens.
Replacing masked positions with negative infinity before softmax makes those positions become zero after softmax.

Dividing by the square root of the head dimension prevents the query–key dot-product variance from growing with dimensionality and helps keep pre-softmax values smaller, which is useful for backpropagation and stable gradients.
In this example, the head dimension is 3 because the output dimension is 6 and the number of heads is 2, so the scores are divided by the square root of 3.
After softmax, each row of the attention weight matrix sums to one.

Because the attention weights in a row sum to one, they can be interpreted as how much attention a token pays to earlier tokens and itself, such as cat paying mostly attention to "the" and only a small amount to cat in the example shown.
The attention weight tensor has the same dimensions as the attention score tensor: batch size, number of heads, number of tokens, and number of tokens.

The full transformation from attention scores to attention weights is to apply a causal mask with negative infinity above the diagonal, divide by the square root of the head dimension, and then apply softmax.
Dropout can also be applied after obtaining attention weights, although it is omitted here for simplicity.
In the code, an upper triangular mask is created and applied to the attention scores so that all elements above the diagonal become negative infinity.
The mask is built only for the context length because the model does not attend to more tokens than the context length at a time.
If a batch contains fewer tokens than the context size, the masking code makes the mask stop at the actual number of tokens.
In the code, the scores are divided by the square root of the last dimension of the keys tensor, which is the head dimension, before applying softmax.
Softmax is applied along the last dimension so that the columns within each row sum to one.
Each element of the attention weight matrix represents the attention weight between a specific query token and a specific key token within a head.
The goal of the attention mechanism is ultimately to compute the context vector matrix.
The context vector matrix is computed by multiplying the attention weights by the value matrix.
The value matrix was computed earlier and is only used in this final step.

For this multiplication, the attention weights have dimensions batch size, number of heads, number of tokens, number of tokens, and the value matrix has dimensions batch size, number of heads, number of tokens, head dimension.
The attention weights matrix can be multiplied by the values matrix because the number of columns in the first matrix matches the number of rows in the values matrix.
Attention weights are different from attention scores because in the attention weights each row sums to one, whereas that is not the case for attention scores.
Multiplying the attention weights by the values produces a context vector output with shape B, number of heads, number of tokens, head dimension.
In the context vector output, each head contains one row per token, and each row is the context vector for that token with dimensionality equal to the head dimension.
The goal is for the final context vector matrix to preserve the D_out dimension, so the number of heads and the head dimension must be merged back together.

To prepare the context vectors for merging into D_out, first swap the number-of-tokens index with the number-of-heads index so the shape changes from B, number of heads, number of tokens, head dimension to B, number of tokens, number of heads, head dimension.

After computing the context vector matrix, transpose the number-of-heads and number-of-tokens dimensions to obtain a context vector matrix with shape B, number of tokens, number of heads, head dimension.
After this transpose, the grouping is by token, and within each token there is one context vector per head.
The reason for the transpose is to bring the number of heads and the head dimension next to each other so they can be merged into D_out more easily.
To combine the results from multiple heads, flatten each token output by merging the outputs of all heads for that token into a single row.
In the final context vector matrix, each row is the context vector for one token, and its length is D_out because the separate head outputs have been merged together.
The final context vector matrix has shape B, number of tokens, D_out.
The code takes the context vector, makes it contiguous in memory, and reshapes it into B, number of tokens, D_out.
Calling contiguous before reshaping is needed to ensure the tensor is in the same memory block so the reshape works properly.
There can be an optional output projection at the end, implemented as a learnable linear layer, although it is not strictly necessary.
This full process produces enriched context vector representations for the tokens.
For larger text, the process is to take sentences, break them into tokens, convert them into token IDs, map them to input embeddings, and then compute context vectors for each token in the same way.
In the demonstration code, there are three tokens, embedding dimension six, D_out equal to six, context length equal to six, dropout rate zero, and two heads.
Dropout in this attention implementation randomly blocks out some attention weights, which is useful for generalization.

For the first batch, the resulting context vector matrix has three rows and six columns, matching the whiteboard example in shape even if the values differ because of different random initializations.
The multi-head attention class can handle multiple batches at once, producing one context vector matrix per batch.
The example uses small embedding sizes and few attention heads only to keep the outputs readable.
GPT-3 uses many more attention heads than this example, and GPT models generally have D_in equal to D_out.
Understanding dimensions and linear algebra is central to understanding and modifying attention mechanisms and to becoming a strong machine learning engineer.
Higher-dimensional matrices become much easier to understand once you write them down and understand what is going on.
You should write things down, such as on a whiteboard or a piece of paper, because doing so helps you remember them for a longer period of time.
The next lecture will start building the LLM model.
